budapest-history-museum.description: The Castle Museum occupies Building E, the southern wing of the Buda Castle palace, and tells the story of Budapest from prehistory to the late twentieth century. Its most distinctive rooms are the restored medieval palace spaces in the basement and a hall of Gothic sculpture found buried in 1974.
paragraphs: The Castle Museum is the part of the Budapest History Museum housed in Building E, the southern wing of the Buda Castle palace, with its main entrance from the Lion Courtyard. Its displays cover roughly two thousand years of the city's past, arranged from the medieval palace in the basement up to prehistory on the top floor.

The basement is the reason many people come. After the damage of the Second World War, archaeologists uncovered the remains of the medieval royal palace beneath the later buildings. The Gothic Hall, built by King Sigismund in the early fifteenth century, is an irregular rectangle of 20.2 by 11.55 metres divided into two naves with rib vaults. Its ribs, pillars, arches and window niches were restored by the sculptor Ernő Szakál in 1961 and 1962, and the architect László Gerő planned the wider reconstruction. Nearby are the palace chapel, stretches of castle wall and a room devoted to the Corvina library.

On the ground floor are the Gothic sculptures from the royal palace. In 1974 a sealed cellar of a townhouse in front of the palace yielded more than sixty sculptural torsos and thousands of fragments from the court of King Sigismund of Luxembourg, who reigned from 1387 to 1437. Some pieces still carry traces of paint, and many were never finished; one guide says the workshop broke up before the work was done, though the reasons remain unclear.

Upstairs, Budapest, Light and Shadow follows about a thousand years of the city's history, while a second exhibition follows the Royal Palace itself from 1686 to today. The top floor, In Pursuit of Lost Times, begins with stone tools about fifty thousand years old and runs to the Hungarian conquest.

The museum has older roots than the castle. Budapest's city assembly decided to found a municipal museum in 1887, and the medieval department and the directorate moved into the restored castle in 1967, after which the whole institution became known as the Budapest History Museum. It also runs the Kiscelli Museum, the Budapest Gallery and the Medieval Jewish Prayer House.
tips: The entrance is in the Lion Courtyard of Building E on the Buda Castle hill; a second entrance leads to the King's Cellar. Check the official site for current opening times and tickets.
The Hungarian National Gallery and the National Széchényi Library are in the same palace complex, so the museum fits easily into a longer castle visit.
One visitor guide notes that the basement level with the medieval rooms cannot be reached by wheelchair; confirm access arrangements on the official page.

kiscelli-museum.description: Set in a Baroque Trinitarian monastery on a plateau above Óbuda, the Kiscelli Museum shows Budapest's urban history from the eighteenth century on and houses the Budapest Municipal Gallery. Its bare-brick former church, now an exhibition and concert space, is the building's most unusual interior.
paragraphs: The Kiscelli Museum stands at Kiscelli utca 108 in Óbuda, on a plateau above Bécsi út, and is a branch of the Budapest History Museum. It presents the history of Budapest from the eighteenth century onward and is also the home of the Budapest Municipal Gallery, the Fővárosi Képtár.

The building began as a Trinitarian monastery. The Baroque complex was built from 1745 to 1758 to designs by the Viennese architect Johann Entzenhoffer, with a church beside the north wing of the two-storey friary. A copy of the Mariazell cult statue was placed there, and the site became a place of pilgrimage known as Kiscell, from the German Klein Zell. One visitor guide gives 1760 as the year the church was consecrated.

In the 1780s, under Joseph II, the order was dissolved; sources give 1783 or 1784. It served as a military hospital, barracks and storage space. Around 1911 (sources give 1910 or 1911) the Viennese furniture manufacturer and collector Miksa Schmidt bought the property and converted it into a mansion, and for a long time it was called the Schmidt Castle. When he died, his will of 1935 left the complex to the capital city for use as a museum.

The Second World War did great damage, and the fighting of November 1956 caused more. A visitor guide reports that the roof was destroyed and that a new one was built between 1976 and 1983, with the church interior deliberately left as bare brick. The former church, with its raw brick nave and empty niches, now hosts large temporary exhibitions and concerts, and the Municipal Gallery held its first exhibition in the ruin in 1988.

The permanent rooms hold some distinctive objects: the original 1712 figures from the Holy Trinity column that stands in front of Matthias Church, a collection of old Pest and Buda shop signs, the complete fittings of the Golden Lion pharmacy and a printing room with a Columbia press. Around the museum lies the Kiscelli park forest, about fifteen hectares of woodland that Schmidt laid out as the mansion's grounds.
tips: A visitor guide lists tram 17 from Széll Kálmán tér, or trams 19 and 41 from Batthyány tér to Szent Margit Kórház, then a steep walk up Kiscelli utca. Bus 165 from Kolosy tér avoids the climb.
One visitor guide says there is no lift and the upper floor cannot be reached by wheelchair, and that some permanent-room labels are in Hungarian only. Check the official site for access details.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and the programme of exhibitions and concerts in the church space.
Allow time for a walk in the Kiscelli park forest around the museum.

budapest-gallery.description: The Budapest Gallery is the contemporary-art arm of the Budapest History Museum. Its exhibition house at Lajos utca 158 in Óbuda occupies an old dwelling house whose recorded history goes back to the early eighteenth century, and it presents Hungarian and international art across painting, photography, design and architecture.
paragraphs: The Budapest Gallery shows contemporary Hungarian and international art, and its exhibition house stands at Lajos utca 158 in Óbuda. The gallery aims to present contemporary art to the public and to introduce Hungarian artists to audiences abroad, and its programme reaches beyond painting to architecture, photography, media art, applied arts and design.

The institution has had several names and homes. It was founded in 1979 as the Budapest Fine Arts Directorate, with one department for public art and one for fine art, and was renamed Budapest Gallery in 1983. In 2011 the city assembly made it a main department of the Budapest History Museum. Its exhibition department first worked from the Klotild Palace building in Szabadsajtó utca and moved in 2013 to the Bálna building on the Danube, where it ran the New Budapest Gallery until 2019.

The Lajos utca house itself has a long and modest history. A museum page records the building as a Bear House at the beginning of the eighteenth century, says it was rebuilt as a dwelling house toward the end of that century, and notes that further extensions were added in the nineteenth century. It is now the gallery's exhibition house.

Besides changing exhibitions of living artists, the house holds a permanent display of works by the sculptor Pál Pátzay, who lived from 1896 to 1976. The small statues in that exhibition, which opened in 1982, come from the Budapest History Museum's own collection. The gallery also looks after the Imre Varga Collection, devoted to another sculptor, which has its own address on Laktanya utca in the same district.
tips: The gallery is in Óbuda at Lajos utca 158; check the official site for the current exhibition programme, opening times and tickets.
Exhibitions change often, so look at the gallery's programme before you travel and see what is on.
The Imre Varga Collection on Laktanya utca is a separate site run by the same gallery, so confirm which venue a given exhibition uses.

hungarian-railway-history-park.description: A railway museum in a former locomotive depot in Budapest's 14th district, with a 34-stall roundhouse, a turntable and more than a hundred vehicles from steam locomotives to rare railcars. Visitors can also try a locomotive simulator and see a small railway running through the grounds.
paragraphs: The Hungarian Railway History Park, Magyar Vasúttörténeti Park, stands at Tatai út 95 in Budapest's 14th district, on the site of the former Northern depot of the Hungarian State Railways. It covers more than 70,000 square metres and displays over a hundred vehicles and pieces of equipment, mostly railway vehicles.

The site has its own history. The depot was built in 1911 as a twin: a 22-stall building and a 34-stall building. Only the larger one survives, because the smaller was destroyed during the Second World War. The surviving roundhouse and turntable now display locomotives, which is why the park is full of engines standing in their old stalls. From 1951 to 1990 the depot carried the name Hámán Kató Fűtőház.

The museum's roots go back further than the park. A small railway open-air museum had operated at Ópaks station in Paks from 1985 to 2000, and the Hungarian Railway Museum Foundation was founded on 22 November 1999. The park itself opened on 14 July 2000.

The fleet runs from steam to electric traction, and some of it still works and is used for nostalgic trips in Hungary and abroad. Named exhibits include a teak dining car built for the Orient Express in 1912, the Árpád railcar of 1934, the steam locomotive MÁV 411.118 of the USATC S160 class and a Soviet GAZ-13 Chaika that served Prime Minister Jenő Fock and was later converted to run on rails.
Visitors can also ride the garden railway in the grounds, which the park's ticket information lists; check the park for its other hands-on attractions.
tips: Nearby bus stops are served by routes 30 and 30A, among others; Angyalföld station is about a 15-minute walk away. Check current routes before you set off.
A halt called Vasútmúzeum on the Budapest to Esztergom line is reported to be served only at weekends and on holidays, so confirm train times if you plan to arrive by rail.
Check the official site for current opening times, tickets and the dates of special events and train rides.

medieval-jewish-prayer-house.description: A small vaulted prayer hall on the ground floor of a house in the Castle District's old Jewish quarter, with Hebrew wall paintings from the Ottoman period and tombstones in a side room off the gateway. Sources differ on how old the hall is, and it is again used for worship.
paragraphs: The Medieval Jewish Prayer House is at Táncsics Mihály utca 26 on the Buda Castle hill, in what was once the Jewish quarter of Buda. The Castle District heritage site describes the building as a single-storey, unpretentious burgher's house that preserves the remains of a medieval Jewish worship hall. It is run by the Budapest History Museum, whose exhibition there is called The Jewish population of Buda in the Middle Ages.

Visitors pass through a barrel-vaulted gateway. In a room to the left stand tombstones from the medieval and Ottoman periods; turning right leads to the worship hall, whose roof is supported by pillars. On the vault is a painting from the Ottoman era showing a drawn bow with a line from Hannah's prayer, The bows of warriors are shattered, and nearby fields with Stars of David carry a priestly blessing from the Book of Numbers.

Sources disagree on the building's dating. Museum and tourism pages say the prayer house was built at the end of the fourteenth century and uncovered in 1964 during monument-protection research, which also revealed seventeenth-century Jewish inscriptions. A 2018 article instead links the hall to the Ottoman period and says it was found in 1968 during postwar reconstruction, starting from two fresco fragments in the gateway. The scholar Sándor Scheiber decoded the lettering and attributed it to Jews of the Sephardic rite rather than the Ashkenazi rite first suspected.

The hall is not the only synagogue site on the street. A far larger Great Synagogue is recorded at number 23, built in 1461 and destroyed in the siege of 1686. Its ruins were found in 1964 by the archaeologist László Zolnay, who reburied them under a concrete slab, and they still lie beneath the courtyard of a Baroque palace.

After years as an exhibition space, the hall was renovated at the initiative of the Unified Hungarian Jewish Congregation and regained its religious function in the autumn of 2018. It holds about seventy people, was designed inside by Tibor Somlai and still serves as an exhibition space on weekdays.
tips: The house is at Táncsics Mihály utca 26 in the Castle District, a short walk from the other Buda Castle sights.
Because the hall is again used for worship, check the official site for current visiting arrangements, opening times and tickets before you go.
It is a small room, so a visit is short; combine it with the Castle Museum, which belongs to the same museum group.

petofi-museum-of-literature.description: Hungary's national literary museum fills the Károlyi Palace, a classicist building where a prime minister was arrested in 1849 and the Hungarian National Council was formed in 1918. Its collections include the manuscript of Petőfi's National Song and a complete Vizsoly Bible, and it reopened in 2023.
paragraphs: The Petőfi Museum of Literature, Petőfi Irodalmi Múzeum, is housed in the Károlyi Palace at Károlyi utca 16, on the corner of Károlyi Mihály utca and Ferenczy István utca. It was founded in 1954 and took over the legacy of the Petőfi–Jókai House, which dated from 1909. Its first two years of exhibitions were held at the Hungarian National Museum, it received a palace at József nádor tér in 1955, and it moved into the Károlyi Palace in the spring of 1957.

The palace is described as one of Budapest's most important classicist monuments. It was rebuilt from 1832 to designs by the Viennese architect Anton Pius Riegl, with József Hofrichter leading the construction, and the new palace was inaugurated in 1841. In the Reform Era it housed the literary salon of László Bártfay, where Franz Liszt played. In January 1849 Lajos Batthyány, prime minister of the first responsible Hungarian government, was arrested there, and in October 1918 the Hungarian National Council was formed in the building.

Count Mihály Károlyi was its last private owner. After he emigrated in 1919 the state confiscated the palace (a heritage register dates this to 1920), and the capital took over the building in the late 1920s, in 1928 or 1929 depending on the source. The capital's picture gallery was based there until 1953, and the Petőfi Museum moved in four years later. Hungarian Wikipedia records auctions of the family's art in 1932 and of a library in 1937. Renovations took place in 1996 to 2000 and again in 2022, and the building reopened in January 2023 with a new permanent Petőfi exhibition.

The collections centre on Hungarian literature. They include the manuscript of Petőfi's National Song, the manuscript of József Attila's poem At the Danube, and a complete copy of the Vizsoly Bible, known as the Károlyi Bible. The museum also holds the literary estates of writers such as Mór Jókai, Zsigmond Móricz, Ferenc Karinthy, Tibor Déry and Antal Szerb, and exhibits a printing press of the Landerer and Heckenast firm.
tips: The palace is at Károlyi utca 16 in central Pest, near the inner-city walking routes; check the official site for opening times and tickets.
Check the official English pages for what is available to non-Hungarian readers, as well as the current exhibitions.

hungarian-agricultural-museum-and-librar.description: Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park is a Romanesque, Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque ensemble designed by Ignác Alpár and built for the 1896 Millennium celebrations. The museum was founded in the same year and holds the national collection on agriculture, hunting, fishing and related food-industry material.
paragraphs: The Hungarian Agricultural Museum occupies the Baroque wing of Vajdahunyad Castle in City Park. The castle was designed by Ignác Alpár and built in 1896 for the Millennium celebrations marking a thousand years since the Hungarian conquest. It was first a set of copies of historical buildings, made mainly of wood and cardboard, and its main façade copies Hunyad Castle in Vajdahunyad, today Hunedoara in Romania, which gave it its name.

The museum itself was founded in 1896. According to Hungarian Wikipedia, the founding decree was signed on 20 June 1896 by the agriculture minister Ignác Darányi, and the museum opened in the castle on 12 September 1897 under its first director, Árpád Balás. The temporary structure was not built to last. It was closed in July 1899 and demolished, and the museum moved to a rented house on Kerepesi út until the castle was rebuilt.

The rebuilding in brick and stone was approved in 1900 and followed Alpár's plans, with the Gothic and Renaissance-Baroque wings finished in 1904 and the Romanesque section in 1908. The museum moved back in 1904, and Franz Joseph I reopened it on 9 June 1907. English Wikipedia gives 1907 for the opening of the exhibition, so the dates in the sources differ slightly. The castle was declared a monument in 1991.

Hungarian Wikipedia reports that the museum has 39 collections and that in 2016 it was estimated to hold more than 400,000 objects. Notable holdings include the first steam locomotive to arrive in Hungary in 1852, a trophy collection and a collection of wheat varieties. In 2015 the Gate Tower and the Apostles' Tower were opened to visitors, and the same year original plans by Alpár were found in a walled-up room.

The courtyard holds Miklós Ligeti's statue of Anonymus, the unknown chronicler at the court of King Béla III, and the Ják Chapel stands in the castle grounds but is not run by the museum. The museum's library has been merged with the national agricultural library, and its holdings in the castle were moved to Attila út in 2019 and 2020.
tips: The castle is in City Park, so it combines easily with a walk around the lake and the other buildings of the park.
Relocation of the museum has been discussed in recent years; check the official site for the current status, opening times and tickets before you go.
The statue of Anonymus stands in the castle courtyard, and the Ják Chapel is in the castle grounds.

hungarian-natural-history-museum.description: Hungary's national natural history museum grew out of collections given to the National Museum in the early nineteenth century. Its exhibition building stands in the Ludovika complex in Pest's eighth district, and its collections cover anthropology, zoology, minerals and fossils.
paragraphs: The Hungarian Natural History Museum, Magyar Természettudományi Múzeum, grew out of the Hungarian National Museum. In 1802 Count Ferenc Széchényi gave his library and coin collection to the nation, and his wife Julianna Festetics later donated a mineral collection that became the root of the natural science collections. Archduke Rainer gave the first palaeontological collection in 1811, and in 1818 the botanical department began with the plant collection of Pál Kitaibel.

Separate departments for zoology, botany and mineralogy were created within the National Museum in 1870. The zoological department moved to a building at Baross utca 13 in 1928, partly because of the 1927 International Zoological Congress in Budapest, and a partly independent natural history museum was set up in 1933. An anthropology department was created soon after 1945, and the museum became independent in 1949.

The 1956 revolution caused heavy losses. The National Museum building was hit on 24 October, destroying parts of the Africa exhibition and mineral and palaeontological material, and on 5 November an incendiary bomb struck the Baross utca building, destroying tens of thousands of specimens and about a hundred thousand books and offprints.

In 1994 the government decided to place the museum in the Ludovika Academy complex, a historic site originally built as a military academy. Collections began moving in from 1995, and the exhibition building opened in 1996. Hungarian sources describe it as the former covered riding hall of the Ludovika, which housed the Alfa cinema after the Second World War; one cinema history says the cinema closed in 1990 and the building was destroyed by arson in 1992, before the museum's renovation. The Ludovika site now houses mineralogy, geology and palaeontology, anthropology, parts of zoology and the library.

The anthropology collection is described as one of the ten largest in Europe. Since 1 July 2024 the museum has been a branch institution of the Hungarian National Museum Public Collection Centre. Moving the museum out of Ludovika has been discussed since 2010 without a move taking place, so its exhibitions are best checked before a visit.
tips: The exhibition site is at Ludovika tér 2 to 6 in the eighth district; the nearest metro stops on line M3 are Semmelweis Klinikák and Nagyvárad tér.
Check the official site for current exhibitions, opening times and tickets, since the museum's future location has been under discussion.
The botanical collection is housed in an Art Nouveau palace on Könyves Kálmán körút that a source says is not open to visitors.

franz-liszt-memorial-museum-and-research.description: On the first floor of the Old Academy of Music on Vörösmarty utca, the museum preserves the apartment where Franz Liszt stayed whenever he was in Budapest from 1881 until his death in 1886. His pianos, desk, library and furniture are displayed in the rooms where he lived.
paragraphs: The Liszt Ferenc Memorial Museum and Research Centre is in the Old Academy of Music at Vörösmarty utca 35, just off Andrássy út. It opened in September 1986 and occupies the building in which the Academy of Music taught from 1879 to mid-1907, after its first four years in a building on Hal tér. The Academy had been founded with Liszt as its founding president and a professor, and he took no salary for his teaching.

Liszt was given a service apartment on the first floor and lived there, whenever he stayed in Budapest, from January 1881 until his death in 1886. The apartment is now the memorial museum, furnished with his instruments, furniture, library and personal belongings. A visitor article notes that the rooms look little changed and that the furniture in the two larger rooms stands where it did in his time.

Look for the walnut writing desk in the corner of the study-bedroom, made for him by his friend the piano maker Ludwig Bösendorfer, with a pull-out three-octave keyboard in place of the middle drawer, which Liszt could use to try out passages. The core collection is Liszt's donation to the Academy and includes a Bösendorfer and two Chickering pianos, a Mason & Hamlin cabinet organ, a combined piano and organ by Erard and Alexandre, and a piano-harmonica by Bachmann. His Budapest library of books and scores is also here.

After the Academy moved to its new palace on Liszt Ferenc tér on 12 May 1907, the building was used by a music school, a coffee shop, associations and a foreign trade company. The Ministry of Culture and Education bought it in 1980 and gave it to the Academy of Music. A first Liszt memorial room had opened in the new Academy building in 1925, and the research centre was founded together with the museum in 1986.

Some key exhibits are on loan from the Hungarian National Museum, which Liszt himself had given important relics from his career. Documents and memorabilia from relatives and pupils, among them Eduard Liszt, Jenő Hubay and István Thomán, have also been added over the decades, together with later purchases and bequests.
tips: The museum is at Vörösmarty utca 35, in front of the Vörösmarty utca stop of the Millennium Underground on Andrássy út.
The concert hall next to the apartment hosts concerts, so check the official site for the current programme, opening times and tickets.
The former dining room and ground-floor foyer are used for temporary exhibitions, so what you see may vary.

ferenc-hopp-museum-of-asiatic-arts.description: A museum of Asian art in the villa on Andrássy út where the optician and collector Ferenc Hopp lived. It grew from his bequest to the state and now holds Chinese, Japanese, Indian, Tibetan and other collections, with a garden that still contains the statues and pagodas he installed.
paragraphs: The Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts is at Andrássy út 103, in the villa and garden that its founder left to the state. Ferenc Hopp, an optician and photographer who took over the Calderoni optical firm in 1864, was born in Fulnek in Moravia in 1833 and died in Budapest on 9 September 1919.

Hopp made five journeys around the world, with a focus on East Asia, especially China and Japan, and he lectured on his travels to the Hungarian Geographical Society. Hungarian Wikipedia says he bought about 1,200 Chinese objects between 1883 and 1914 and that his Japanese collection numbered nearly 2,000 items at his death. His collection also drew on Africa, America and Australia, but East Asian art was the standout.

In 1919 he left the villa, the garden and several thousand objects to the state. Sources give the number as about 4,000 to more than 4,500 items. His will required that the building be used as an East Asian art museum and that the museum always bear his name. It opened in 1923, and its collection has grown through gifts, purchases and transfers from other museums, including the Zichy North Asian collections and the Indian collection of Imre Schwaiger.

The collection now covers China, Japan, India, Southeast Asia, Nepal, Tibet, Mongolia, Korea and the Middle East. Japanese medieval art and Chinese bronzes and porcelain are especially significant. Hungarian Wikipedia gives about 23,000 objects in 2006, while a 2021 article says about 30,000, so the figure depends on the source. After 1945 the museum also received state gifts from Vietnam, China and North Korea.

The villa garden still holds the Asian statues, pagodas and memorial columns that Hopp erected. The museum is part of the Budapest World Heritage site and is a specialist museum of the Museum of Fine Arts.
tips: The museum is on Andrássy út at number 103, a stretch of the avenue with several other museums and villas near the City Park end.
Temporary exhibitions focus on individual Asian countries and peoples; check the official site for what is on, plus opening times and tickets.
Allow a few minutes to walk around the garden, which is part of what Hopp left to the state.

mary-magdalene-tower.description: The Mary Magdalene Tower is the surviving part of a Gothic parish church on Kapisztrán tér in the Castle District. The church was used by Hungarians in medieval Buda, became a mosque under the Ottomans, and was demolished after the 1945 siege. The tower reopened to visitors in July 2025 under district council management, so check its current status.
paragraphs: The Mary Magdalene Tower stands on Kapisztrán tér in the Castle District, close to Matthias Church. It is all that remains of the Church of Mary Magdalene, one of two large churches of medieval Castle Hill. The Matthias Church served the German community, while the Magdalene church was the parish church of Buda's Hungarians.

The Castle District heritage site says the parish was formed in the mid-thirteenth century as a chapel of the parish of the Matthias Church, with a small single-nave first church. By the end of the fifteenth century the late Gothic church had six vault sections, an enlarged chancel and a five-storey tower, built by the town's Hungarian community. During the Ottoman era it was the only Christian church on the castle hill, shared by Catholics and Protestants, until the Fifteen Years War, when it became a mosque.

After the siege of 1686 only the tower remained usable. The Franciscans cleared the Gothic remains and built a Baroque church and monastery, and the tower was repaired in Baroque style. Francis I was crowned Hungarian king in the church in 1792, in 1817 it was given to the Buda garrison, and in 1920 it became the church of the Roman Catholic Military Bishopric.

The siege of 1944 and 1945 brought down the vaults of the nave and sanctuary. Repairs began but full restoration never happened, and when the military bishopric ceased the church had no maintainer. Reconstruction of the tower began in 1950, at the same time as the church building was demolished. A porch built for the coronation of Francis I survives, as does a late Gothic gate leading to a star-vaulted lower storey.

The former churchyard is now an archaeological park, sealed off by a glass wall, and the site of the church is a garden of ruins with a reconstructed sanctuary window. A news report says the tower opened to tourists in 2017, that the district council withdrew the previous operator's concession in early 2025 and the tower closed in February 2025, and that it reopened on 15 July 2025 under the council's own management. Its present status should be checked.
tips: The tower closed in February 2025 and, according to a July 2025 news report, reopened on 15 July 2025 under the first district council. Check the official site or the district's pages for its current status before you plan around a climb.
One visitor guide mentions buses 16, 16A and 116 and the Castle District funicular as ways to reach the area.
Even when the tower itself is closed, the ruins garden and the surrounding square are close to Matthias Church and the Fisherman's Bastion.
